text:
Alfred North Whitehead was born in Ramsgate, Kent, England, in 1861. He was educated at Sherborne, excelling in sports and mathematics, and attended Trinity College, Cambridge, where he graduated as a fourth wrangler in 1884. He became a fellow of Trinity and taught mathematics and physics at the college until 1910, during which time he spent the 1890s writing his *Treatise on Universal Algebra* (1898) and collaborated with Bertrand Russell on *Principia Mathematica* (1910–1913).
Moving to the United States in 1924, Whitehead taught at Harvard University and produced significant philosophical works, including *Science and the Modern World* (1925) and *Process and Reality* (1929). His philosophy is known as "process philosophy," which rejects "scientific materialism" and posits that reality is composed of fundamental, interrelated "occasions of experience" rather than static matter. He developed the term "prehension" to describe perception, and his concept of God is characterized as a "dipolar" entity that is both permanent and fluent, interacting with the world. Whitehead also made significant contributions to educational theory, advocating for a transdisciplinary approach over teaching "inert ideas."
